title.value: Structural Evolution of the Buena Vista and Elk Hills Anticlines and Hydrocarbon Trapping Potential (South San Joaquin Basin, California)

note.value:
The goal of this study was to provide a structural model for the Buena Vista (BV) and Elk Hills (EH) anticlines (Fig. 1) and to add new insights into timing and possible mechanisms of trap formation. The interpretation was based on balanced restoration of a cross-section running from north of EH through BV and up to the San Andreas Fault in the south. GeoSec2D was used to visualize and model critical points, as fold geometry in connection to observed fault shape and slip amount, differences in forelimb/backlimb dips, and thinning of stratigraphic horizons across anticlines.

GeoSec2D was also used to unfold the studied cross- section in steps corresponding to each stratigraphic top. This enabled the reconstruction of the incremental strains, the calculation of the amount of shortening, and the prediction of possible structural features required by the kinematic constraints and by the observed structural geometries.

As a general concluding remark, the BV and EH anticlines can be interpreted in 2D as folds related to a deep decollement with flat-and-ramp geometry. The space problems observed during unfolding have been attributed to a young episode of wrenching. However, thrusting was still required during wrenching in order to account for the present fold geometry. Therefore the overall structural picture can be interpreted as generated due to thrusting followed by transpression. This is a new interpretation for the structures associated with the San Andreas fault in the south San Joaquin basin, which differ from both the pure wrenching (Harding, 1976, Nicholson, 1990) and the pure thrusting (Davis and Lagoe, 1988) models. Based on this interpretation, the EH and BV differ substantially from other features located further south and north along the same structural trend, i.e., Wheeler Ridge (Medwedeff, 1992; Mueller and Suppe, 1997), Lost Hills (Medwedeff, 1989; Wickham, 1995), and Kettleman Hills (Bloch et al., 1993). This difference indicates the high variability in strain behavior and kinematic style along the San Andreas Fault. For exploration activities, the association of thrusting and wrenching can provide additional structural trapping potential which might be underestimated based on the previous structural models.

Girbacea, Radu. (2000). Structural Evolution of the Buena Vista and Elk Hills Anticlines and Hydrocarbon Trapping Potential (South San Joaquin Basin, California). Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/bj044sg1924
